title: Java Programming Foundations

target.learner: A tertiary fresher or independent beginner with basic computer literacy and no assumed programming experience
target.professionalOutcome: Write, run, debug, verify, document, and publish small dependency-free Java programs with enough fluency for introductory practical examinations and beginner projects.

assumptions: The learner has a Windows computer and basic file, browser, and typing skills.
No prior programming, command-line, Git, Java, testing, or object-oriented knowledge is assumed.
Setup is separate from the eight instructional Weeks and may be skipped capability by capability after verification.
Required learning resources are free to access; a free verified GitHub account is needed only for final repository publication.
Most project work can continue offline after the required tools and referenced materials have been opened or downloaded.

setup.description: Install and verify the smallest Windows Java toolchain used throughout the course. Skip only a capability whose verification checks already pass.

capabilities.description: Install IntelliJ IDEA, select the intended JDK, and run a saved Java class.

capabilities.title: Free GitHub account

Create a free personal account if needed.

phases.title: Run and Reason
phases.outcome: Build a correct mental model of Java execution, typed values, diagnostics, decisions, iteration, arrays, and lists.

phases.title: Organize Behavior and State
phases.outcome: Use methods, objects, files, exceptions, debugging, and checks to make dependable small programs.

phases.title: Integrate, Verify, and Share
phases.outcome: Assemble, document, inspect, and publish a reproducible Java command-line project.

competencies.name: Prepare and verify a Java workspace
competencies.description: Create an IntelliJ Java project with the intended JDK, identify the source root, and run a saved class.

competencies.name: Explain source, compilation, and execution
competencies.description: Distinguish a .java source file, compiler feedback, bytecode, the JVM, a class, and a main entry point at beginner depth.

competencies.name: Read and repair early Java errors
competencies.description: Use IntelliJ/compiler messages, file and line evidence, and a stack trace to repair syntax, name, type, or runtime failures.

competencies.name: Represent values with Java types
competencies.description: Declare readable int, double, boolean, char, and String variables; distinguish primitives from references at beginner depth.

competencies.name: Read and convert console input
competencies.description: Use one Scanner deliberately, read text and numeric input without newline surprises, and parse numeric text when appropriate.

competencies.name: Compare Java values correctly
competencies.description: Use numeric comparisons, boolean operators, and String.equals instead of reference equality for text decisions.

competencies.name: Express ordered decisions
competencies.description: Use if/else-if/else in a deliberate order so invalid, boundary, and successful cases produce one explainable result.

competencies.name: Recover from invalid numeric text
competencies.description: Catch NumberFormatException only around the expected conversion boundary without hiding unrelated defects.

competencies.name: Repeat with progress and stopping rules
competencies.description: Use for and while loops, deliberate updates, break, and traceable stopping conditions without accidental infinite loops.

competencies.name: Process fixed arrays
competencies.description: Create, index, update, and traverse a fixed-length array while respecting zero-based boundaries.

competencies.name: Manage a growing ArrayList
competencies.description: Create a typed ArrayList, add/get/remove values, inspect size, and traverse without unsafe index changes.

competencies.name: Define focused static methods
competencies.description: Write static methods with purposeful names, parameters, return types, and one understandable responsibility.

competencies.name: Return and compose values
competencies.description: Return values rather than relying on incidental printing and combine focused methods into a larger result.

competencies.name: Reason about local scope and overloads
competencies.description: Keep local variables inside their method boundary and distinguish a changed argument list from a changed return type.

competencies.name: Create simple Java objects
competencies.description: Define a class, constructor, private instance fields, and independent instances with valid initial state.

competencies.name: Encapsulate object behavior
competencies.description: Expose focused methods that validate and change one object while preserving its invariants and unrelated instances.

competencies.name: Use object collections
competencies.description: Store typed objects in an ArrayList and query or summarize them through public methods.

competencies.name: Read and write UTF-8 text with Files
competencies.description: Use Path and Files with a stable project-relative location, explicit UTF-8, and predictable line records.

competencies.name: Handle file and conversion failures narrowly
competencies.description: Distinguish a missing first-run file, malformed stored record, and I/O failure without erasing existing data.

competencies.name: Debug one failing case in IntelliJ
competencies.description: Set a breakpoint, step through one reproducible failure, inspect local values, repair one cause, and rerun the same case.

competencies.name: Verify behavior with a dependency-free check harness
competencies.description: Run deterministic normal, boundary, and invalid cases through small check methods without adding a build framework.

competencies.name: Parse a small command-line contract
competencies.description: Read command-line arguments, validate command shape and values, and provide usable help without ambiguous input.

competencies.name: Document and publish a safe Java repository
competencies.description: Write reproducible JDK/IntelliJ/run instructions, inspect staged paths, commit locally, and push a secret-free project to GitHub.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Java source is checked and compiled before the JVM runs the resulting class instructions.
concepts.example: `javac Main.java` reports compile errors before `java Main` can run.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating an old successful run as proof that the edited source compiled.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A beginner console application starts in a class method named main with the required signature.
concepts.example: `public static void main(String[] args)` is the entry point.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing the method name or omitting static and expecting the launcher to find it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A compiler error or stack trace names a location, type, and message that narrows the repair.
concepts.example: A missing semicolon is reported at or near the affected statement.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing multiple unrelated lines before reading the first useful diagnostic.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Every Java variable has a declared type that constrains values and operations.
concepts.commonMistake: Putting quoted numeric text into an int without conversion.

concepts.simpleMeaning: String.equals compares text content; == compares whether references identify the same object.
concepts.commonMistake: Using == for user-entered text.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Scanner reads console input, and mixing token and line methods requires deliberate newline handling.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling nextInt then nextLine without accounting for the pending line ending.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Parsing converts valid numeric text and throws a specific exception for invalid text.
concepts.commonMistake: Catching every Exception around the whole program.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An if/else-if/else chain chooses the first matching branch.
concepts.example: Reject invalid ages before testing eligibility.
concepts.commonMistake: Putting a broad success condition before a required rejection.

concepts.simpleMeaning: && and || evaluate left to right and may skip the right operand once the result is known.
concepts.commonMistake: Using | or & without understanding eager evaluation.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A while loop needs an update that can move its condition toward false.
concepts.example: Increment acceptedCount only after a valid record.
concepts.commonMistake: Incrementing the wrong counter and never reaching the stop rule.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An array has fixed length and indexes from zero through length minus one.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading scores[scores.length].

concepts.simpleMeaning: An enhanced for loop visits each value when the index itself is unnecessary.
concepts.commonMistake: Trying to resize the array through the loop variable.

concepts.simpleMeaning: An ArrayList stores a growable ordered collection of one declared element type.
concepts.commonMistake: Mixing unrelated value types or using size as the last index.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A method contract states parameter types, return type, and one responsibility.
concepts.example: `static double subtotal(List<Double> prices)` returns a number.
concepts.commonMistake: Collecting input, calculating, saving, and printing in one method.

concepts.simpleMeaning: return sends a compatible value to the caller and ends that invocation.
concepts.commonMistake: Printing when the caller needs the value.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A local variable exists only inside its declaring block.
concepts.example: A subtotal inside calculateTotal is not visible in main.
concepts.commonMistake: Relying on hidden mutable fields instead of parameters and returns.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Overloads share a name but differ by parameter list, not only return type.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing only the return type and expecting a valid overload.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A constructor establishes one new object’s initial field values.
concepts.commonMistake: Using shared static state for per-book availability.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Private fields protect state while public methods provide controlled operations.
concepts.commonMistake: Making every field public and allowing invalid transitions.

concepts.simpleMeaning: this names the receiving object and distinguishes its fields from parameters.
concepts.commonMistake: Assigning `title = title` and leaving the field unchanged.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A typed list can hold objects and call their public methods while traversing.
concepts.commonMistake: Duplicating object fields in unrelated parallel arrays.

concepts.simpleMeaning: Path identifies a location; Files performs explicit text I/O at that location.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming the working directory without recording it.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A missing first-run file differs from an existing line that cannot be parsed.
concepts.example: No file may start empty; a malformed line must stop without overwrite.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating every load failure as an empty first run.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A catch should handle only an expected failure at the smallest useful boundary.
concepts.commonMistake: Catching Exception and continuing with corrupt state.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A breakpoint pauses before a suspicious statement so values and control flow can be inspected.
concepts.example: Pause before a counter update and inspect index and total.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding random edits before reproducing one stable case.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A small check compares actual and expected behavior and fails visibly on mismatch.
concepts.commonMistake: Changing the expected value just to make a check pass.

concepts.simpleMeaning: The args array contains tokens supplied after the class name and must be validated before use.
concepts.example: `java Main add "Finish lab"` produces three argument tokens as defined.
concepts.commonMistake: Reading args[0] before checking the length.

concepts.simpleMeaning: A repository is reviewable when tracked files and README let another learner compile, run, and verify it safely.
concepts.example: README gives exact JDK, IntelliJ, javac/java, and check commands.
concepts.commonMistake: Publishing IDE caches, credentials, private records, or undocumented commands.

resources.title: Install the free core of IntelliJ IDEA on Windows

location.start: Begin at Install IntelliJ IDEA and read the unified-product note plus Windows system requirements.
location.stop: Stop at the working Welcome screen; do not buy Ultimate, install optional plugins, alter the bundled runtime, or enable remote development.
location.note:
Do: Install the current Windows release for the current user, launch it, choose the free core after any Ultimate-trial prompt, and reach the Welcome screen. Record the installed version from Help | About.

Finished when: IntelliJ IDEA opens on Windows and its free Java core remains usable without payment.

Next: Create the verification project and obtain the standalone JDK inside the IDE.

resources.whySelected: The current unified-product guide explicitly confirms that core Java functionality remains free and documents supported Windows installation without requiring an Ultimate subscription.

resources.title: Create a Java project and download JDK 25 in IntelliJ

location.start: Begin at Create a new Java project.
location.stop: Stop after the regular Main class runs; compact source files, packages, JAR artifacts, Maven, Gradle, and paid IDE features are outside Setup.
location.note:
Do: Create `java-setup-check` with Java, the IntelliJ build system, and JDK 25; use Download JDK if needed. Under `src`, create a regular `Main` class with `public static void main(String[] args)`, print `Java setup ready`, run from the gutter, and locate the output plus exit code 0.

Finished when: A saved regular Main.java runs with JDK 25 and the learner can point to src, the Run window, program output, and exit code.

Next: Open PowerShell and run `java --version` and `javac --version`; both should report 25 before continuing.

resources.whySelected: The current IntelliJ tutorial joins project creation, the standalone JDK 25 download, source-root recognition, build, run, bytecode output, and exit code in one maintained route.

resources.title: Install Git and configure commit identity

location.start: Begin at Using Git.
location.stop: Stop before GitHub authentication, repository creation, commits, or pushes; those actions are taught when the final project is ready.
location.note:
Do: Install Git for Windows if needed, configure the intended global name and email, then verify `git --version`, `git config --global user.name`, and `git config --global user.email` in PowerShell.

Finished when: Git runs in PowerShell and can attribute a later local commit to the intended learner identity.

Next: Verify or create the free GitHub account.

resources.whySelected: GitHub maintains the Windows installation and local identity checklist required before the Week 8 repository is published.

resources.title: Create or verify a free GitHub account

location.start: Begin at About your personal account on GitHub.
location.stop: Stop at the working profile page; do not select a paid plan, organization product, Copilot subscription, or repository yet.
location.note:
Do: Create a free personal account if needed, verify the email address, sign out, and sign in once. Store no password or token in a course project.

Finished when: The learner can sign in to a verified free GitHub account for Week 8 publication.

Access: Creating a verified free personal GitHub account is the outcome; no paid plan is required.

Next: Begin the first Core Week 1 resource.

resources.whySelected: The official guide documents a verified free personal account without making a paid plan part of the learning contract.

resources.title: See IntelliJ build and run a regular Java class

location.start: Begin at Build and run the application, then use Convert the compact source file into a regular class only to see the regular form.
location.stop: Stop before packages and JAR packaging; do not use compact source syntax in the weekly Build.
location.note:
Do: Read Build and run, create the course-required regular `public class Main` and standard main signature directly, run it, find the generated `out` directory, and write one sentence each for source, compiler, bytecode, JVM, output, and exit code.

Finished when: You can distinguish Main.java, compilation, Main.class bytecode, JVM execution, output, and exit code.

Next: Watch the visual first-application walkthrough and reproduce its project navigation actions.

resources.whySelected: The current official tutorial visibly connects a saved source file, javac compilation, generated bytecode, the JVM run, output, and exit code inside the course IDE.

resources.title: Video walkthrough: your first Java application

location.start: Start the embedded Your First Java Application video at the beginning.
location.stop: Stop once the class runs from the gutter and the Run window shows the expected labelled output; do not package a JAR.
location.note:
Do: Watch through creating the project/class, writing main, running, and locating output. Pause after each action and repeat it in a disposable `video-practice` class; ignore packaging/JAR work if it appears later.

Finished when: You can navigate to src, create a regular class, identify main, run it, and locate output without copying a complete project.

Next: Use the compiler page to prove what javac creates outside the IDE.

resources.whySelected: JetBrains’ free visual walkthrough demonstrates project navigation, class creation, main, run controls, and the Run window; those stable fundamentals still match the current IDE workflow.

resources.title: Compile source into bytecode with javac

location.start: Begin at Introducing javac and Description.
location.stop: Stop after repairing the semicolon and obtaining a clean compile; modules, annotation processing, cross-compilation, class paths, and extra options are outside this course.
location.note:
Do: Read through the .java/.class naming explanation and the `-d` option only. From the project root run `javac -d out src/Main.java`, confirm `out/Main.class`, delete one semicolon, rerun the same command, and record the first message plus location.

Finished when: You can identify the compiler input/output and use the first reported source location for one minimal repair.

Next: Read how the java launcher finds main and reports a runtime stack frame.

resources.whySelected: The official compiler page states exactly how .java source becomes .class bytecode and explains the `-d` destination option used by the Week 1 PowerShell route.

resources.title: Launch main and read runtime evidence

location.start: Begin at Introducing the Java Tool and read Description through the main-method declaration.
location.stop: Stop after the repaired terminal run; source-file mode, JARs, modules, VM tuning, and advanced launcher options are outside Week 1.
location.note:
Do: Run `java -cp out Main`, compare it with the javac step, set the supplied divisor to zero, rebuild, rerun, and annotate exception type, message, and the first `Main.java` frame before restoring the divisor.

Finished when: You can explain that javac reports compile failures while java/JVM execution can produce a runtime exception and stack frame.

Next: Take the Week 1 Skill Check, then create the Student Introduction and Study-Time Card.

resources.whySelected: The official launcher page defines the required main signature, JVM launch step, and argument boundary without collapsing compilation and execution into one unexplained button.

resources.title: Declare Java primitive values and Strings

location.start: Begin at Primitive Types.
location.stop: Stop before numeric ranges beyond int/double, unsigned operations, hexadecimal/binary literals, underscores, arrays, var, and wrapper-class detail.
location.note:
Do: Read static typing, int/double/boolean/char, the String note, local-variable initialization, and character/String literals. Type a small `TypesPractice` class; predict then print every value and record the two rejected assignments.

Finished when: You can choose among int, double, boolean, char, and String and explain why String is not a primitive.

Next: Learn the exact line-oriented Scanner boundary used by the Campus Profile Collector.

resources.whySelected: The official bounded page defines static typing, primitive values, String’s reference-type status, literals, local initialization, and the exact quote rules needed this Week.

resources.title: Read complete console lines with Scanner

location.start: Read the Scanner class summary, then jump directly to nextLine().
location.stop: Stop after restoring the all-nextLine version; delimiters, regex searching, locales, streams, and multiple Scanners are outside Week 2.
location.note:
Do: Create one `Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in)`, read three complete lines, echo them with labels, and run with a two-word name. In a disposable copy, call `nextInt()` before `nextLine()` once and record why the apparently skipped line occurs.

Finished when: You can explain why nextLine returns the rest of the current line and why consistent line reads prevent a pending-newline surprise.

Next: Convert the age text and then learn content-safe String comparison.

resources.whySelected: The JDK 25 API defines Scanner token versus line behavior precisely, letting beginners avoid the common nextInt/nextLine pending-newline trap by reading lines consistently.

resources.title: Compare String content with equals

location.start: Open the String API at equals(Object).
location.stop: Stop before compareTo, Collator, regex, locale-aware comparison, and overriding equals in custom classes.
location.note:
Do: Read the equals contract and its return condition only. Run a small example comparing the same input with `==` and `.equals`, predict both results first, and replace the incorrect comparison in the profile program.

Finished when: You can select `.equals` for user-entered text and explain why `==` is not a content comparison for String references.

Next: Use JShell to trace typed declarations, parsing, and two comparison forms.

resources.whySelected: The official JDK contract states exactly that String.equals compares the character sequence, supporting the Week 2 repair without introducing custom object equality.

resources.title: Interactive trace: input text, parsed number, and equality

location.start: Begin at Example of Starting and Stopping a jshell session and Example of Entering Snippets.
location.stop: Stop after the five predictions are corrected; saved scripts, external libraries, startup configuration, JavaFX, and replacing the weekly project with JShell are outside this course.
location.note:
Do: Start `jshell` in IntelliJ Terminal, enter `String ageText = "19"`, `int age = Integer.parseInt(ageText)`, `age + 1`, `new String("yes").equals("yes")`, and `new String("yes") == "yes"`. Predict each type/value before Enter, use `/list`, then `/exit`.

Finished when: You can distinguish quoted text, parsed numeric value, arithmetic, content equality, and reference equality from observed results.

Next: Take the Week 2 Skill Check, then build the Campus Profile Collector.

resources.whySelected: JShell is included with the JDK and provides a no-account feedback loop for inspecting expression types and values without replacing the saved IntelliJ project.

resources.title: Combine comparisons with short-circuit Boolean operators

location.start: Begin at The Equality and Relational Operators, then read The Conditional Operators.
location.stop: Stop before ternary, instanceof, bitwise, shift, and operator-precedence detail not used by the Build.
location.note:
Do: Run the comparison example and a three-part eligibility expression. Predict each Boolean result; add a small method call on the right of && to observe that it is skipped when the left side is false.

Finished when: You can write readable range/eligibility conditions and explain why && or || may not evaluate its right operand.

Next: Put invalid, boundary, and successful cases in an intentional if/else-if order.

resources.whySelected: The official operators lesson joins relational, equality, logical complement, and short-circuit &&/|| behavior in runnable examples that match the eligibility rules.

resources.title: Order if, else-if, and else branches

location.start: Begin at The If-Then Statement and continue through The If-Then-Else Statement.
location.stop: Stop before while, for, break, continue, return, and switch; loops arrive in Week 4.
location.note:
Do: Run `IfElseDemo`, predict the grade before execution, then adapt it to check invalid age first, missing prerequisite second, low score third, and eligible last. Exercise ages 15, 16, 120, and 121.

Finished when: You can justify the branch order and show that one input produces exactly one result.

Next: Learn how parseInt reports invalid numeric text.

resources.whySelected: The official grade example demonstrates that the first true branch wins, the exact model needed to reject invalid input before testing success.

resources.title: Convert numeric text and identify NumberFormatException

location.start: Open Integer.parseInt(String) and read its Parameters, Returns, and Throws contract.
location.stop: Stop before radix overloads, unsigned parsing, decoding, boxing caches, and other Integer methods.
location.note:
Do: Run parseInt with `"50"`, `"-1"`, `""`, `"4.5"`, and `"fifty"` one at a time. Record which produce an int and which throw NumberFormatException; preserve the original text in the record.

Finished when: You can predict parseInt outcomes and name NumberFormatException as the expected failure for invalid integer text.

Next: Wrap only that expected conversion in a matching catch.

resources.whySelected: The JDK 25 method contract explicitly names the successful result and NumberFormatException conditions, grounding recovery in the actual conversion boundary.

resources.title: Catch an expected conversion failure narrowly

location.start: Begin at Catching and Handling Exceptions, then jump to Practicing Basic Try-Catch.
location.stop: Stop before multi-catch, finally, try-with-resources, custom exceptions, and catching `Exception`; those are not required by this Week.
location.note:
Do: Run the basic example, adapt it to catch only NumberFormatException around `Integer.parseInt`, print one clear invalid-input result, and prove a separate programming defect is still visible. Sketch the call stack from the thrown conversion to main.

Finished when: You can recover from expected invalid numeric text without hiding unrelated compile or runtime defects.

Next: Take the Week 3 Skill Check, then build the Course Registration Eligibility Checker.

resources.whySelected: The official try/catch lesson includes runnable basic and multiple-handler practice while supporting the course rule that unrelated defects must not be swallowed.

resources.title: Repeat deliberately with while, for, for-each, and break

location.start: Begin at The While and Do-while Statements, then read The for Statement and The break Statement.
location.stop: Stop before labeled break/continue, return, switch, and nested-loop exercises; do-while is recognition only and is not required in the Build.
location.note:
Do: Run one while loop with an explicit counter, one indexed for loop, and one enhanced for loop. Create a three-column trace for condition, body effect, and update; use an unlabeled break only for a documented sentinel.

Finished when: You can select a loop form, show its progress, and explain how its stopping rule becomes false or reaches break.

Next: Store a fixed probe set in an array and respect zero-based boundaries.

resources.whySelected: The official control-flow page demonstrates loop conditions, updates, enhanced for, infinite-loop risk, and unlabeled break in one maintained source.

resources.title: Create, index, and traverse fixed arrays

location.start: Begin at Arrays and read through Using the Length of an Array, then open Practicing Array Creation and Manipulation.
location.stop: Stop before multidimensional arrays, arraycopy, copyOfRange, sorting, and advanced array calculations.
location.note:
Do: Create `int[] scores = {55, 70, 85, 100}`, print first and last using `0` and `length - 1`, total with for-each, and deliberately inspect the failure at `scores[scores.length]` before repairing it.

Finished when: You can traverse a fixed array and state that its valid indexes are zero through length minus one.

Next: Compare the fixed array with a typed list that grows as scores are accepted.

resources.whySelected: The official array lesson explicitly teaches fixed length, zero-based indexing, length, initialization, and both indexed and for-each traversal with runnable practice.

resources.title: Use a typed ArrayList for a growing ordered list

location.start: Begin at Exploring the List Interface and Choosing your Implementation of the List Interface.
location.stop: Stop before sorting, subList, immutable factories, LinkedList performance, iterators, streams, and concurrent modification detail.
location.note:
Do: Read through the basic indexed List operations and Practicing List Operations. Recreate only add, get, set, remove, size, and for-each with four Integer scores; predict the list after every change.

Finished when: You can explain why ArrayList can grow, why size is not a valid last index, and when a fixed array remains sufficient.

Next: Practice collection membership and mutation while keeping loop indexes valid.

resources.whySelected: The official List lesson explains ordered indexed data, why ArrayList is the beginner default, and common get/set/add/remove operations without requiring streams.

resources.title: Practice safe ArrayList operations and summary loops

location.start: Begin at Methods That Handle Individual Elements.
location.stop: Stop before bulk operations, removeIf, toArray, predicates, lambdas, streams, sets, maps, and implementation performance.
location.note:
Do: Run the add/remove/contains examples with Integer scores. Then traverse an unchanged list to calculate count, total, min, and max; test an empty list separately before any division or first-element read.

Finished when: You can mutate a typed list intentionally, summarize it safely, and avoid using size as an element index.

Next: Take the Week 4 Skill Check, then build the Classroom Score Tracker.

resources.whySelected: The official practice examples make add, remove, contains, size, and iteration observable before the learner combines input validation and summaries.

resources.title: Define focused methods and valid overloads

location.start: Begin at Defining a Method and continue through Overloading Methods.
location.stop: Stop before arbitrary arguments, command-line parameters, and reference-type mutation; Week 5 needs only ordinary typed parameters and restrained overloads.
location.note:
Do: Read the declaration components, naming guidance, and overload section. Write `static double subtotal(double price, int quantity)` and `static double subtotal(double price, int quantity, double discountRate)`, then prove a return-type-only duplicate fails to compile.

Finished when: You can identify a method signature, choose a return type, and explain why changed return type alone is not overloading.

Next: Trace how arguments enter parameters and why local variables do not escape their method.

resources.whySelected: The official method lesson decomposes modifiers, return type, name, parameter list, body, signature, and overload rules, including why return type alone cannot distinguish an overload.

resources.title: Pass arguments into typed parameters

location.start: Begin at Passing Information to a Method or a Constructor and read Parameter Types, Parameter Names, and Passing Primitive Data Type Arguments.
location.stop: Stop before varargs, reference data type arguments, constructors, inheritance, and object mutation; those arrive when objects are introduced.
location.note:
Do: Recreate the primitive pass-by-value example with a cafe quantity. Draw caller and callee boxes, predict the values before running, and rename any shadowing local that makes the trace unclear.

Finished when: You can distinguish argument from parameter and explain why reassigning an int parameter does not change the caller variable.

Next: Return values to the caller and compose small calculations.

resources.whySelected: The official lesson distinguishes parameters from arguments and shows Java pass-by-value behavior, giving beginners a concrete model for local method state.

resources.title: Return values and keep local scope visible

location.start: Begin at Declaring Classes and focus only on the class body, fields versus method bodies, method declarations, and returned values in the Bicycle example.
location.stop: Stop before inheritance, interfaces, nested classes, access-control design, and constructors; objects begin in Week 6.
location.note:
Do: In a disposable class, write `subtotal`, `discountAmount`, and `finalTotal` methods that return double values. Compose them in main; then try to print a method-local variable from main, record the compiler error, and repair the design by using the return value.

Finished when: You can compose returned values and keep each local variable within its declaring method/block.

Next: Trace a complete cafe quote through four small method calls.

resources.whySelected: The official class declaration example places fields, methods, parameters, returns, and method bodies together, allowing a bounded exercise that contrasts returned results with block-local variables.

resources.title: Interactive trace: decompose a cafe quote

location.start: Review Example of Entering Snippets, then start a clean `jshell` session.
location.stop: Stop after `/methods` shows the intended contracts and `/exit` closes the session; varargs, lambdas, classes, external dependencies, and production use of JShell are outside Week 5.
location.note:

skillCheck.title: Run, Read, and Repair Java Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: PowerShell is open in the project folder. `javac -d out src/Main.java` has succeeded. Which command runs the compiled `Main` class from `out`?

options.label: `javac out/Main.class`
`java src/Main.java out`
`java -cp out Main`
`Main.java -cp java`

questions.explanation: `java -cp out Main` tells the Java launcher to search the `out` class path for the compiled Main class. `javac` compiles source; it does not run a class.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes a normal beginner Java run?

options.label: Save `.java` source, compile it, then let the JVM run the resulting class instructions
Run the JVM first, then ask it to create the source file
Convert the source directly into a README, then execute the README
Open a `.class` file in the editor and compile it back into `.java`

questions.explanation: The saved `.java` file is source. Compilation checks it and produces class instructions, which the JVM can then execute.

questions.prompt: Which method declaration gives the Java launcher the standard entry point used in this week’s console application?

options.label: `public void start()`
`static int main()`
`public Main(String[] args)`
`public static void main(String[] args)`

questions.explanation: For this course’s console programs, the launcher looks for `public static void main(String[] args)`. A constructor or differently named method is not that entry point.

questions.prompt: A missing semicolon prevents `javac` from producing an updated class. Later, a validly compiled program divides an integer by zero and stops. How should the two failures be classified?

options.label: Both are compile failures because they appear in source
The semicolon issue is a compile failure; division by zero is a runtime failure
The semicolon issue is a runtime failure; division by zero is a compile failure
Both are runtime failures because the learner noticed them while trying to run

questions.explanation: The compiler rejects invalid Java syntax before execution. Integer division by zero is discovered only when the compiled statement runs.

questions.prompt: After one missing semicolon, the compiler prints several messages. What is the strongest first repair move?

options.label: Rewrite every line that appears after the error
Delete the output folder and ignore the message
Change the project JDK without checking the source location
Read the first useful message and location, repair that source line, then compile again

questions.explanation: One syntax mistake can cause later messages. Repairing the earliest useful reported cause and recompiling keeps the diagnosis evidence-led.

questions.prompt: Nneka changes the printed learner name in IntelliJ, but PowerShell still shows the old name. The run command is correct. What should she verify first?

options.label: That the JDK has been reinstalled since the edit
That the class was renamed after the earlier run
That the source was saved and recompiled before the rerun
That the terminal screen was cleared before running

questions.explanation: The JVM runs compiled class instructions, not unsaved editor text. Saving and recompiling ensures the run reflects the current source.

questions.prompt: A run ends with `ArithmeticException: / by zero` and includes `at Main.main(Main.java:9)`. Which evidence most directly identifies where the application failed?

options.label: `Main.java:9`, together with the exception type and message
Only the word `Exception`, without its type or source frame
The last successful compiler command from an earlier run
A Java-library frame that does not name the application source

questions.explanation: The exception states the failure, while `Main.java:9` points to the application source line executed when it occurred.

questions.prompt: The source contains `public class Main` but is saved as `Student.java`. The compiler reports that Main should be declared in a file named Main.java. What is the smallest repair?

options.label: Add a second `main` method
Save the public `Main` class in `Main.java`
Change every printed value to text
Run the mismatched file repeatedly

questions.explanation: A public top-level class must match its source filename. Saving this class as `Main.java` satisfies the reported rule without unrelated edits.

questions.prompt: `javac` reports no errors for a program that calculates weekly study time. What has this result established?

options.label: The program meets every learner requirement
The arithmetic result is guaranteed correct
The source passed compilation, but behavior still needs to be run and checked
The project has already been published safely

questions.explanation: Successful compilation establishes that the compiler accepted the source. It does not prove that the program’s result or requirements are correct.

questions.prompt: A compile message points to one missing semicolon, while the learner also wants to reformat several output lines. Which sequence gives the clearest evidence?

options.label: Repair the reported semicolon, recompile the same case, then make separate formatting changes
Reformat everything and assume the semicolon was included
Suppress compiler output before editing
Replace the whole class with an unrelated example

questions.explanation: A single targeted repair followed by the same compile attempt shows whether the reported cause was fixed. Unrelated changes make that result harder to interpret.

skillCheck.title: Types, Strings, Scanner, and Conversion Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A learner’s planned sessions must be stored as the whole number `3`. Which declaration matches that value?

options.label: `boolean sessions = 3;`
`int sessions = 3;`
`char sessions = "3";`
`String sessions = true;`

questions.explanation: `int` stores whole-number values such as 3. The other declarations pair incompatible types and values.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly stores one grade letter and a course name?

options.label: `String grade = 'A'; char course = "Java";`
`char grade = "A"; String course = 'Java';`
`int grade = A; boolean course = Java;`
`char grade = 'A'; String course = "Java";

questions.explanation: A `char` literal uses single quotes and contains one character. A `String` literal uses double quotes and can contain multiple characters.

questions.prompt: The learner may enter the full name `Ada Lovelace`. Which Scanner call reads that complete line, including the space?

options.label: `scanner.nextLine()`
`scanner.hasNextInt()`
`scanner.close("Ada")`
`scanner.equals("Ada Lovelace")`

questions.explanation: `nextLine()` reads the remaining characters on the current line, so a multiword name stays together.

questions.prompt: Code calls `nextInt()` for age and immediately calls `nextLine()` for course. The course becomes empty. What caused the surprise?

options.label: `nextLine()` converts course names to numbers
`nextInt()` closes the Scanner automatically
`nextInt()` leaves the line ending for the following `nextLine()` to consume
`String variables cannot hold spaces

questions.explanation: Token methods such as `nextInt()` do not consume the line ending. The next `nextLine()` may therefore read only that leftover ending.

questions.prompt: Which pattern keeps this week’s text input predictable while still producing an integer age?

options.label: Read age with `nextLine()`, then pass the text to `Integer.parseInt`
Read age with `nextInt()`, then immediately read course with `nextLine()` and ignore the pending ending
Store the numeric-looking text directly in an `int` without conversion
Call `nextLine()` twice and always discard the first response

questions.explanation: Reading one complete line and converting it deliberately avoids mixing token and line boundaries while making the conversion visible.

questions.prompt: What value does `Integer.parseInt("18")` produce when the text is valid?

options.label: The String `"Integer"`
The boolean `true`
The int value `18`
The char value `'1'`

questions.explanation: `Integer.parseInt` converts valid whole-number text into an `int`. It does not preserve the quotation marks.

questions.prompt: The variable `answer` contains user-entered text. Which condition checks whether its content is exactly `yes`?

options.label: `answer = "yes"`
`answer.equals("yes")`
`answer >= "yes"`
`answer + "yes"`

questions.explanation: `String.equals` compares text content. Assignment and arithmetic operators do not perform that content test.

questions.prompt: A learner uses `answer == "yes"` and sees inconsistent text decisions. What is the core problem?

options.label: `==` compares text after converting it to numbers
`==` compares text without respecting letter case
`==` compares String length rather than its characters
`==` compares String references, not their text content

questions.explanation: For Strings, `==` asks whether two references identify the same object. `equals` is the intended content comparison.

questions.prompt: What value is stored by `int hours = 95 / 60;`?
questions.explanation: Both operands are integers, so integer division keeps the whole-number quotient: 1. The remainder would require a separate `%` calculation.

questions.prompt: The program has `String ageText = scanner.nextLine();` and then needs numeric arithmetic. Which next statement preserves a clear conversion boundary?

options.label: `int age = Integer.parseInt(ageText);`
`String age = ageText + 1;`
`boolean age = scanner.equals(ageText);`
`char age = ageText;`

skillCheck.title: Decide, Validate, and Recover Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A registration checker must reject ages outside 16–120 before deciding eligibility. Which branch should appear first after successful numeric conversion?

options.label: The successful-eligibility condition
The score-threshold condition
The prerequisite-failure condition
The invalid-age range check

questions.explanation: An invalid age is not an ordinary eligible or ineligible case. Rejecting it first prevents later rules from assigning a misleading result.

questions.prompt: A valid score includes both 50 and 100. Which condition identifies a score inside that range?

options.label: `score > 50 && score < 100`
`score >= 50 && score <= 100`
`score == 50 || score == 100`
`score < 50 && score > 100`

questions.explanation: `>=` and `<=` include both boundary values, while `&&` requires the score to satisfy the lower and upper rules together.

questions.prompt: An `if/else if/else` chain has two conditions that would be true, but the first one matches. What happens next?

options.label: Both matching blocks run
The last matching branch replaces the first result
Only the first matching block runs; later branches are skipped
The compiler chooses one matching block at random

questions.explanation: An ordered chain selects its first true branch. Later `else if` and `else` blocks in that chain do not run.

questions.prompt: A learner is eligible only when the score is at least 50 and the prerequisite is complete. Which expression states both requirements?

options.label: `score >= 50 && hasPrerequisite`
`score >= 50 || hasPrerequisite`
`!score >= 50`
`score = 50 && "yes"`

questions.explanation: `&&` is true only when both operands are true. `||` would accept a learner who meets only one requirement.

questions.prompt: In `age >= 16 && hasId`, `age >= 16` is false. What does short-circuit `&&` allow Java to do?

options.label: Evaluate `hasId` and use that value alone
Evaluate `hasId` twice to confirm the result
Skip evaluating the right operand because the whole expression is already false
Treat the skipped right operand as a compile error

questions.explanation: For `&&`, one false operand makes the complete expression false. Java therefore need not evaluate the right operand.

questions.prompt: Which handler belongs directly around `Integer.parseInt(scoreText)` when `"fifty"` is an expected invalid entry?

options.label: `catch (NumberFormatException error)`
`catch (ArithmeticException error)` around every branch
`catch (Exception error)` around the whole application
`catch (NullPointerException error)` around printing

questions.explanation: `Integer.parseInt` reports invalid numeric text with `NumberFormatException`. Catching that expected failure at the conversion keeps unrelated defects visible.

questions.prompt: A large `try` block parses a score, compares rules, and prints results, then catches `Exception` as “bad score.” Why is that unsafe?

options.label: It changes `NumberFormatException` into an I/O failure
It makes every later `else` branch execute
It is rejected because Java permits only one statement inside `try`
It may disguise an unrelated programming defect as an input mistake

questions.explanation: A broad catch can intercept failures caused by defective code, not just bad numeric input. The protected boundary should remain narrow and specific.

questions.prompt: An age is invalid when it is below 16 or above 120. Which expression matches that rejection rule?
questions.explanation: Either out-of-range condition is enough to reject the age, so the two alternatives are joined with `||`.

questions.prompt: A learner enters `fifty` where a numeric score is required. Which result best preserves the checker’s contract?

options.label: Report invalid numeric input rather than classifying the learner as ineligible
Treat the text as score zero and continue silently
Approve the learner because the word describes 50
Catch every future error and always print success

questions.explanation: Conversion did not produce a valid score, so eligibility rules cannot yet be applied. Invalid input is a separate outcome from valid-but-ineligible data.

questions.prompt: The first branch says `if (score <= 50) invalid`, and a later branch says `else if (score >= 50) eligible`. What happens to the valid boundary score 50?

options.label: It reaches the eligible branch because both are true
It skips the complete chain
It is captured by the first branch and wrongly reported invalid
It causes NumberFormatException

questions.explanation: At 50, the first condition is true, so later branches are skipped. The invalid condition should reject values below the accepted boundary, not the boundary itself.

skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A tracker should keep asking until the learner enters `done` or five valid scores have been accepted. Which loop best represents that changing stop rule?

options.label: A `while` loop whose condition depends on the accepted count, with a `break` for `done`
A `for` loop that always runs exactly five times, including rejected entries
One `if` statement that checks `done` only once
An enhanced `for` loop over an empty score list before scores are collected

questions.explanation: A `while` loop fits repetition controlled by changing state. Its body must update that state or break when the sentinel appears.

questions.prompt: A loop says `while (accepted < 5)` but never changes `accepted` and has no reachable `break`. What is the main defect?

options.label: The array has too many element types
The loop automatically skips its first run
The condition may remain true forever
The compiler changes `accepted` after each print

questions.explanation: Without a state update or stopping branch, the condition can remain true indefinitely and create an accidental infinite loop.

questions.prompt: For a nonempty `scores` array, which expression reads its final element?

options.label: `scores[scores.length]`
`scores[scores.length - 1]`
`scores.length - 1`
`scores[last]`

questions.explanation: Array indexes start at zero, so the final valid index is one less than the array length.

questions.prompt: An array contains three values. What happens when code evaluates `scores[3]`?

options.label: It returns the third value
It expands the array by one slot
It returns zero without warning
It fails at runtime because valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2

questions.explanation: The length is 3, but the last valid index is 2. Index 3 lies outside the fixed array boundary.

questions.prompt: The program only needs to add every score and never uses its position. Which loop is the clearest fit?

options.label: `while (scores)`
`for (int score : scores)`
`if (int score = scores)`
`for (scores.length : score)`

questions.explanation: An enhanced `for` loop visits each array value directly when the index itself is not part of the work.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates a growable list intended to contain only Integer values?

options.label: `int scores = new int[];`
`ArrayList scores = 0;`
`String<Integer> scores = new String<>();`
`ArrayList<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();`

questions.explanation: `ArrayList<Integer>` declares the element type, while `new ArrayList<>()` creates the growable list instance.

questions.prompt: An `ArrayList<Integer>` contains four scores. Which expression retrieves its final score?

options.label: `scores.get(scores.size())`
`scores[scores.length - 1]`
`scores.get(scores.size() - 1)`
`scores.last()`

questions.explanation: `size()` is the number of elements, so the final zero-based index is `size() - 1`. ArrayList access uses `get`.

questions.prompt: The program first stores exactly three diagnostic probe scores, then accepts an unknown number of valid classroom scores. Which pairing fits those needs?

options.label: Use an array for the three probes and an ArrayList for the growing accepted scores
Use ArrayList for the fixed probes and forbid additions to the unknown collection
Use two fixed arrays and guess a very large second length
Use a String for probes and a boolean for accepted scores

questions.explanation: An array expresses a known fixed length. An ArrayList fits an ordered collection whose size grows as valid values are accepted.

questions.prompt: A learner enters 140, but only scores from 0 through 100 are accepted. What should happen to the list and accepted-count state?

options.label: Append zero in place of 140
Append 140 but leave the count unchanged
Increment the count but do not append
Neither should change until a valid score is accepted

questions.explanation: Rejected input is not an accepted score. Updating either state would make the collection or count disagree with the stated contract.

questions.prompt: Inside the score-entry loop, when should `break` run under this week’s contract?

options.label: After every invalid numeric value
When the normalized input is `done`, ending entry deliberately
Before the first prompt appears
Whenever one score is below the current average

questions.explanation: `break` implements the explicit `done` sentinel. Invalid entries are rejected and the loop can continue without pretending the session is finished.

skillCheck.title: Methods, Returns, and Decomposition Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A class already contains `static double subtotal(double price, int quantity)`. Which line calls that method with a price of 750.0 and quantity 2?

options.label: `static double subtotal(double price, int quantity)`
`subtotal = static double`
`subtotal(750.0, 2)`
`return type subtotal price quantity`

questions.explanation: The method name followed by compatible arguments performs the call. The declaration separately defines the method’s parameter and return contract.

questions.prompt: For `static double fee(double amount, boolean takeaway)`, what are `amount` and `takeaway`?

options.label: Arguments permanently stored in the JVM
Parameters that receive values supplied by each call
Classes created whenever the method runs
Exceptions thrown before compilation

questions.explanation: Parameters are named, typed inputs in the method declaration. A call supplies matching argument values for one invocation.

questions.prompt: The caller must subtract a discount amount while calculating a quote. Which ending makes the discount helper composable?

options.label: `System.out.println(discount);` only
`discount == true;`
`new Scanner(discount);`
`return discount;`

questions.explanation: `return discount` sends the calculated value to the caller. Printing alone shows output but does not provide a value for the formula.

questions.prompt: A method declares `static double calculateFee(...)`, but one branch reaches the closing brace without returning a value. What should the compiler report?

options.label: A return value may be missing on that path
The compiler inserts `0.0` for the missing branch
Only the first branch’s return type is checked
The method silently changes to `void` for that branch

questions.explanation: A non-void method promises a compatible value to every completing call. Each reachable completion path must honor that return contract.

questions.prompt: `double subtotal` is declared inside `calculateSubtotal`. Which statement about that local variable is correct?

options.label: It is shared permanently across all method calls
It automatically becomes a field on every object
It can be read from any class without a return value
It exists only within its declaring method/block and is not directly available in `main`

questions.explanation: A local variable belongs to its declaring block. Returning its value lets a caller use the result without exposing the local name.

questions.prompt: A class already defines `format(int value)`. Which additional declaration can form a valid overload?

options.label: `String format(double value)` with a different parameter type
`int format(int value)` with the same parameter list
`String format(int value)` differing only by return type
`void format(int value)` differing only by parameter name spelling

questions.explanation: Overloads need different parameter lists, such as `int` versus `double`. Changing only the return type or parameter name does not create a distinct signature.

questions.prompt: Which design makes `calculateSubtotal` easiest to reuse in several quote cases?

options.label: Have it create a Scanner, ask every question, print, and save a file
Have it read global mutable fields set by unrelated methods
Pass the needed prices and quantities in, then return the subtotal
Make it exit the application after one calculation

questions.explanation: Explicit parameters and a returned value give the helper one clear calculation responsibility. Input and presentation can remain in `main`.

questions.prompt: The methods return `subtotal = 2500`, `discountAmount = 250`, and `feeAmount = 200`. Which expression calculates the quoted total without double-counting?

options.label: `subtotal + subtotal - feeAmount`
`subtotal - discountAmount + feeAmount`
`subtotal * discountAmount * feeAmount`
`discountAmount - subtotal + feeAmount`

questions.explanation: Start with the subtotal, subtract the returned discount amount once, and add the returned fee amount once: 2450.

questions.prompt: `main` and `calculateTotal` are both declared `static` in the same class. Which ordinary call is appropriate inside `main`?

options.label: `double total = calculateTotal(subtotal, discount, fee);`
`double total = new static calculateTotal;`
`return main.calculateTotal;`
`class total = calculateTotal;`

questions.explanation: A static method in the same class can be called by its name with matching arguments; the returned value can be assigned to a compatible variable.

questions.prompt: A method named `calculateDiscount` also prompts for input, writes a receipt, and changes the menu. What is the smallest principled improvement?

options.label: Rename it `doEverything` and keep all dependencies hidden
Duplicate the method for every possible customer
Catch every exception so the responsibilities cannot fail
Let it receive required values and return only the discount; move input and output to their callers

questions.explanation: A focused calculation contract makes the method understandable and composable. Prompting and receipt output belong at a different boundary.

questions.prompt: The class declares `Book(String title)`. Which expression creates a new Book whose title starts as `Kindred`?

options.label: `Book book = Book.title("Kindred");`
`Book book = new Book("Kindred");`
`new String = Book(Kindred);`

options.label: Both unavailable because methods are shared
The first unavailable and the second available
The first still available and the second unavailable
Both replaced by one static Book

questions.explanation: Each instance has its own availability field. Sharing method code does not require sharing the per-object state that the method changes.

questions.prompt: A Book is already unavailable. Which checkout sequence best protects that state contract?

options.label: Set available false again, then decide whether the action was valid
Change every Book so the list stays consistent
Return success without inspecting the field
Check availability first; reject the invalid transition without mutating, otherwise change the field

questions.explanation: Validation should precede mutation. A rejected checkout leaves the original unavailable state unchanged and reports the failed operation clearly.

questions.prompt: Why keep `available` private and expose `checkout()` and `returnBook()` methods?

options.label: The methods validate allowed changes before updating private state
Callers can still assign the private field after validation
Public methods make constructor state checks unnecessary
The private field becomes one value shared by all Books

questions.explanation: Private state narrows direct access. Public behavior can validate transitions and preserve the class’s rules before changing that state.

questions.prompt: After declaring `static boolean available`, checking out one Book makes every Book appear unavailable. What caused the defect?

options.label: Constructor parameters are shared by default
ArrayList copies the first element’s state into later elements
`this` points to the class instead of the current object
The static field belongs to the class, so all instances share it

questions.explanation: A static field is class-level state. Availability describes one Book, so it should be an instance field initialized separately for each object.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates a growable collection intended to hold only Book references?

options.label: `Book books = new int[10];`
`ArrayList<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();`
`ArrayList<String> books = new Book();`
`static books = ArrayList<boolean>;`

questions.prompt: Inside `for (Book book : books)`, which expression asks each Book for its display text through a public method?

options.label: `Book.displayLine = books;`

`book.displayLine()`
`private displayLine(book);`

questions.explanation: The enhanced loop variable refers to one Book at a time. Calling `book.displayLine()` invokes that instance’s public behavior.

questions.prompt: The first checkout succeeds. A second checkout of the same Book is rejected by the method. What state should remain after the rejected call?

options.label: The Book becomes available again
The title is erased
Every Book is removed from the collection
That Book remains unavailable

questions.explanation: The invalid transition should be detected before mutation. Rejection therefore preserves the already-unavailable state.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes `Book` from `new Book("Kindred")`?

options.label: `Book` defines the type and behavior; `new Book(...)` creates one initialized instance
They are two spellings for the same local variable
`Book` is a runtime exception and `new Book` catches it
`Book` is an ArrayList and `new Book` is an array index

questions.explanation: The class defines the structure and available behavior. A constructor call with `new` creates one object that follows that definition.

skillCheck.title: Files, Exceptions, Debugging, and Checks Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates the roles of `Path` and `Files`?

options.label: Path opens and closes every file; Files stores the path as plain text
Path validates record fields; Files chooses the application’s working directory
Path contains the file data; Files contains only the filename
Path names a location; Files provides operations that read or write at that location

questions.explanation: A Path represents where the program intends to work. Files contains the operations that act on that path.

questions.prompt: Why should the note store use UTF-8 explicitly for both writing and reading?

options.label: It guarantees every record follows the application format
It prevents another process from deleting the text file
Both operations use the same documented encoding across environments
It reconstructs Java objects from each stored line

questions.explanation: Using the same explicit encoding makes character interpretation predictable across machines. Encoding does not validate the record’s application structure.

questions.prompt: Which pair describes two different load outcomes that should not share the same recovery?

options.label: No notes file on the first run; an existing line missing required fields
An empty ArrayList; another empty ArrayList
Two valid records with different titles
Two successful reads of the same UTF-8 file

questions.explanation: A missing first-run file can legitimately mean no saved notes yet. An existing malformed line means stored data could not be interpreted and needs protective handling.

questions.prompt: Loading stops because one existing record has the wrong number of fields. What should the program do before any save?

options.label: Treat the complete file as empty and overwrite it
Report the malformed record and leave the existing file unchanged
Append a success message to the malformed line
Delete the file so the next run looks like a first run

questions.explanation: Malformed data is not evidence that the file is empty. Refusing to overwrite preserves evidence and prevents accidental loss while the cause is repaired.

questions.prompt: A loader reads lines and converts an ID field. Which design keeps failure meaning clearest?

options.label: Wrap the whole application in `catch (Exception)` and continue
Catch every failure and return an empty list
Catch I/O around the file operation and numeric conversion around the ID parsing boundary
Ignore all failures because the file is local

questions.explanation: Narrow handlers preserve the distinction between file access trouble and malformed numeric content, while leaving unrelated defects visible.

questions.prompt: A saved note receives the wrong ID after `nextId` is updated. Where is the most useful first breakpoint?

options.label: Only after the wrong ID has been saved and the method has returned
Immediately before the suspicious ID assignment or update
At the first line of `main`, even if many unrelated steps occur before the failure
On output-formatting code that runs after the ID has already changed

questions.explanation: Pausing before the suspected state change exposes the current values and control path that lead to the wrong ID.

questions.prompt: At the breakpoint, `nextId` is 4 but becomes 6 after one method call. Which next action best narrows the cause?

options.label: Change the expected ID to 6 immediately
Add broad exception handling around the debugger
Restart repeatedly without inspecting execution
Step into or over the call while watching the relevant local values

questions.explanation: Stepping across the suspected call while inspecting values shows exactly where the unexpected update occurs. The expectation should not be changed without contract evidence.

questions.prompt: A check reports `first id — expected 1, actual 2`. What does that result establish?

options.label: For this named case, observed behavior differs from the stated expectation
The expected value must be changed because actual output is authoritative
The file write failed before any ID was calculated
Every note-creation path is defective in the same way

questions.explanation: The check identifies one reproducible mismatch between expected and actual behavior. Investigation must determine whether code or expectation violates the contract.

questions.prompt: The contract says the first note ID is 1, and debugger evidence shows code increments before assignment. What is the principled repair?

options.label: Change expected 1 to expected 2
Move the increment, then rerun the unchanged check
Delete the failing check
Catch AssertionError and print success

questions.explanation: The expectation matches the stated contract and the debugger exposed the implementation cause. Repair the update order and verify against the same case.

questions.prompt: After repairing the ID update found by one failing check, which sequence provides the strongest evidence?

options.label: Publish immediately because the debugger closed
Rerun only a different successful case
Rerun the same failing case, then run the complete check harness
Replace every expected value with the latest output

questions.explanation: The focused rerun verifies the specific cause; the full harness checks that the repair did not break other established behaviors.

questions.prompt: Why should `main` check `args.length` before reading `args[0]`?

options.label: A run with no arguments has no element at index 0 and should receive help instead of an index failure
Java inserts an empty command at index 0 unless length is checked
`args[0]` always contains the class name and must be skipped
Checking length converts every remaining argument to its required type

questions.explanation: The args array may be empty. Validating its shape first prevents out-of-bounds access and lets the program provide a usable command message.

questions.prompt: Under the documented contract, the learner runs `java -cp out Main complete 7`. Which token should be treated as the command and which as the task ID text?

Command `7`; ID `out`
Command `java`; ID `Main`
Command `complete`; ID `7`

questions.explanation: Tokens after the class name populate args. Here `args[0]` is `complete` and `args[1]` is the task ID text to validate and convert.

questions.prompt: The user enters `archive`, but the CLI supports only `add`, `list`, `complete`, and `help`. What response best preserves the command contract?

options.label: Treat `archive` as `add` without telling the user
Report the unknown command and show the valid command forms
Create a new command dynamically with no tests
Delete the task file and start again

questions.explanation: A clear rejection plus valid usage lets the user correct the command without guessing or triggering unintended behavior.

questions.prompt: The `complete` command receives an unknown task ID and no valid state change exists. What should happen to the task file?

options.label: Replace it with an empty file
Append the invalid ID as a completed task
Leave it unchanged and report the rejected operation
Save a partially modified in-memory list

questions.explanation: An invalid operation should not create persisted state. Reporting the rejection while preserving the existing file protects valid tasks.

questions.prompt: Which check gives the strongest evidence for the `complete 7` command?

options.label: Run the command once and accept any output that contains 7
Use known starting tasks, then compare expected and actual state and message
Change the stored task manually after the command
Inspect only whether the source file is long enough

questions.explanation: A known starting state and explicit expected result make the command behavior deterministic and repeatable without depending on prior manual runs.

questions.prompt: Which README instruction is most reproducible for another learner at the project root?

options.label: Open IntelliJ and click Run without naming the configuration
Compile and run with whichever Java command is familiar

Open Main.java and assume the IDE selects the intended JDK

questions.prompt: Why inspect `git status --short` before and after staging the project?

To record the project JDK inside every staged source file

With generated IntelliJ caches preloaded
